paras: The Taylorville jail mob of 1882 was a series of attempts by crowds in Taylorville, Christian County, Illinois, to lynch Lee Pettis, John C. Montgomery and Emanuel Clementi, three men accused of assaulting schoolteacher Emma Bond. After threats against the jail in early July, a crowd of thousands took the prisoners from the jail about midnight on August 11-12 and hoisted Montgomery by the neck to force a confession, but returned all three to jail alive. Papers across the country followed the case, first presuming the men lynched and then printing detailed accounts of their pleas of innocence.

On the afternoon of June 29, 1882, Emma Bond was reported attacked at the Raymond schoolhouse near Taylorville, held in the attic for hours and left badly injured. First reports blamed 'two tramps', but suspicion turned to three young men living within a few hundred yards of the school, Montgomery, Pettis and Clementi, who had helped take Bond home in a wagon that night. The case against them, as the Cheyenne Leader summarized it, was circumstantial: they had been away from home 'on the pretense of fishing', were said to dislike the teacher, and Clementi wore low shoes and red stockings like a man Bond glimpsed. They were arrested on July 1, along with John Montgomery's brother William.

A July 1 dispatch said a thousand men had gathered at the Bond home and that 'Judge Lynch will probably settle the affair'. On July 3, with Montgomery released on bail and Pettis still in jail, a mob was on the streets, and the sheriff telegraphed Governor Cullom that the jail was threatened. The governor told him to call out a posse and ordered Capt. Culver's local militia company to stand ready. On the night of July 5 a warning of a raid from Blue Mound led the company to guard the jail until morning, but no attack came.

The preliminary hearing ended on August 11 with William Montgomery released and the other three held for the grand jury on bail of $3,000 to $4,000. Spectators moved toward the prisoners when the decision was announced but were checked by the sheriff and his posse. According to a detailed Chicago account, a crowd of 2,000 or 3,000 waited quietly around the jail for 'an organized party' and then, urged on by a few drunken men, forced its way in after the sheriff abandoned the building. Pettis and Montgomery were pulled through an opening in the top of a cell, a new rope was thrown around their necks, and the mob tried with blows and threats to make them confess.

The crowd dragged the two men to the jail yard and then to the courthouse yard, where Montgomery was pulled about four feet off the ground and held there for a minute. He and Pettis kept declaring their innocence, and Clementi, found later, was held on the other side of the yard. When Montgomery was about to be hoisted again, Bond's father, A. D. Bond, cut the rope. A barn fire in the western part of town then drew much of the crowd away, and Bond and the prosecuting attorney persuaded the rest to return the prisoners to their cells.

A Springfield dispatch the next day reported regret in Taylorville at the mob's 'lawless proceedings' and a growing opinion that the men were innocent. Threats did not end: late in August Bond's father wrote that his daughter's death would be 'the signal for the immediate lynching' of the three, and bail was arranged though the men were said to prefer 'safety inside the jail'. They gave $4,000 bail each in early September and returned to their farms south of Blue Mound, while a Blue Mound special reported a Tower Hill vigilance committee secretly preparing to hang them and a fourth suspect, Dr. Vermillion.

In December a grand jury indicted both Montgomerys, Pettis, Clements and Vermillion, and a change of venue to the Montgomery circuit put off the trial until April 1883. No arrest or prosecution of any member of the mob, and no report of the trial's outcome, appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers through Springfield, St. Louis and Chicago wire dispatches reprinted from New York and Washington to Nevada, Dakota and Montana. Headlines named the accused 'the Violators of Miss Bond' and 'The Outragers of Miss Bond', and the St. Paul Globe's first August report presumed 'Their Lives Evidently Cut Short by a Rope'. Several papers looked forward to the lynching: the Northern Pacific Farmer predicted 'a tight rope performance at Taylorville', and the Cairo Bulletin in southern Illinois wrote of the mob's threat, 'That threat should be carried out'.

The New York Sun's long account, also carried in Cheyenne, quoted the prisoners' pleas of innocence and described them as 'Tortured by Blows and Hanging', while still calling them 'wretches'. The Manitowoc Pilot charged that Governor Cullom, by asking for particulars instead of sending troops, 'wanted to give the lynchers a chance'. No report states the race of the accused men or of the mob; one variant of the July wire called Bond 'a colored school teacher', a phrase absent from the same dispatch in other papers.

Accounts differ on the size of the August crowd, given as 2,000 or 3,000 by the Sun and 3,000 to 4,000 by the Evening Star. They also differ on who was hoisted: the Sun names only Montgomery, the Ottawa Free Trader says Clementi received 'the same treatment', and a St. Louis bulletin says the mob alternately hanged and lowered all three.

bases: Crowds threatened the Christian County jail in early July and on the night of August 11-12 a mob took three accused men from it, put ropes around their necks and hoisted one from a tree to force confessions, but killed no one (A4, A16, A17).

A mob of thousands seized John Montgomery, Lee Pettis and Emanuel Clementi from jail on the accusation of assaulting Emma Bond and hanged Montgomery for about a minute, but all three were returned alive to jail (A16, A17, A27); it was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The July jail threat is carried by separate Taylorville and Springfield dispatches (A4, A5, A9), and the August seizure by independent Springfield, St. Louis and Chicago dispatches that agree on the core events (A15, A16, A17, A22).
